title: The Glasshouse of Milton Flats
premise: Paloma Dunmore, a night librarian in the insomniac city of Milton Flats, has spent five years nearly telling her family why she left home — until Ezequiel Vann, the last fluent speaker of a dying trade-tongue called Kesswa, asks her to become his final student. As she learns the language, she discovers it was her own grandmother's tongue too, and that the Dunmore family fortune was built on silencing it. When the last bus route to the old neighborhood is slated for rerouting, Paloma must finally ask the question her family arranged itself around — what happened the night her grandmother stopped speaking — and in doing so loses her inheritance but gains the words to rebuild.
about_author: Lena Okonkwo is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories from disappearing communities before turning to fiction. She writes about language, memory, and the quiet violence of families from a small apartment above a laundromat.

chapters.title: The Hours Nobody Claims
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Working the night shift at Milton Flats Central Library, Paloma catalogs a donation of cassette tapes labeled in an alphabet she almost recognizes. The emotional beat is restless recognition — something buried stirring. She pockets one tape instead of logging it, a small theft that signals how much she already knows and refuses to say.

chapters.title: A Man Who Speaks to Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. She traces the tapes to Ezequiel Vann, living alone in the condemned Glasshouse building, and he offers to teach her Kesswa — his final student, he says, or none at all. The beat is wary hope. Their first lesson reveals he knew her grandmother, and Paloma's practiced art of almost saying things begins to crack.

chapters.title: What the Dunmores Arranged
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. At her mother's Sunday dinner, Paloma watches the family's careful choreography around an empty chair and an unspoken name. Her brother Theo warns her off 'that old man's stories.' The beat is suffocating politeness; the reader sees a family built like architecture around a missing room.

chapters.title: Kesswa Has No Word for Sorry
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Lessons deepen: Kesswa turns out to encode obligation and debt in its grammar, and Ezequiel reveals the Dunmore mills paid workers in scriba while banning their language on the floor. The beat is dawning anger. Paloma realizes her inheritance is literally the price of her grandmother's silence.

chapters.title: The Rerouting
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. The city announces the 47 bus line — the last route through the old neighborhood — will be discontinued, severing the Glasshouse from the city. Ezequiel's health falters; Theo's development firm stands to profit from the rezoning. The beat is urgency closing in from all sides, time becoming a character.

chapters.title: Tape Eleven
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. She finally plays the stolen tape: her grandmother's voice, young, singing, then cutting off mid-word as another voice — her grandfather's — threatens her. The beat is devastating clarity. Paloma understands the question she must ask, and that asking it will cost her everyone at that Sunday table.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Development Office
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Rising action peaks as Paloma confronts Theo with the tape, demanding he halt the rezoning and acknowledge what their grandfather did. He offers her money instead — the family's oldest answer. The beat is betrayal sharpened into resolve; she refuses, and the family begins arranging itself against her.

chapters.title: The Last Full Lesson
chapters.summary: POV: Ezequiel. In his voice for the first time, we learn his own guilt — he testified against the mill owners and was paid to leave town, abandoning Paloma's grandmother mid-lesson. Now dying, he gives Paloma the question in Kesswa, whole. The beat is grief braided with transmission; the torch passes.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Climax: at the final public hearing on the bus reroute, with the family seated behind her, Paloma rises and asks her grandmother's question aloud — first in English, then in Kesswa, her grandmother's recorded voice answering through the library tapes she plays into the microphone. The beat is rupture and release; the room's arrangement breaks permanently.

chapters.title: Glasshouse, Lit
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Resolution: the reroute is delayed, the Glasshouse granted landmark status as a language house; Ezequiel dies having heard Kesswa spoken by three people, not two. Paloma, disinherited and unburdened, opens free evening classes in the old neighborhood. The beat is earned quiet — not restoration, but a beginning built on finally saying it.
